title: Transversality And Intersection
notes: Open the chapter by naming the central machine: make a map transverse, get a finite or one-dimensional preimage, and then count what cannot change under homotopy. The lecture should feel like a sequence from local coordinates to global consequences, not a collection of isolated theorems.

title: Chapter Dependency Map
notes: Use the dependency map to preview how the arguments fit. Boundary coordinates explain why compact one-manifolds have paired endpoints. Transversality turns geometric meetings into regular finite sets. Mod two parity then survives homotopy, and that invariant powers winding, separation, and antipodal coincidence.

title: Boundary Charts Remember One Missing Side
notes: Stress that a boundary point is not a singularity. It has a smooth chart, but the local model is a half-space rather than all of Euclidean space. The inward normal coordinate gives the extra bookkeeping used later when a one-dimensional preimage meets the boundary of a parameter interval.

title: Compact One-Manifolds Are Parity Devices
notes: This slide is the chapter's parity engine. A compact one-manifold is built from circle and interval components, so its boundary has an even number of points. Every later mod two invariance proof is a dressed-up use of this census.

title: Transversality Makes Intersections Regular
notes: Read the formula as a tangent-space spanning condition. At a point mapping into the target submanifold, the derivative of the map and the tangent directions of the submanifold together fill the ambient tangent space. When that happens, the inverse image is itself a clean submanifold of the expected dimension.

title: Tangency Is The Pair-Creation Event
notes: Use the line and circle picture as the small model for nontransverse behavior. At tangency the count is unstable, but on the transverse sides intersection points are born or die in pairs. The ordinary count jumps by two, while the mod two count is unchanged.

title: A Homotopy Sweeps A One-Manifold
notes: Explain the homotopy proof geometrically. A one-parameter family of transverse maps defines a swept inverse image inside the product with the interval. Its boundary consists of the two endpoint intersection sets, and compact one-manifold parity says those endpoint counts agree modulo two.

title: Mod Two Intersection Number
notes: Present the invariant as intentionally modest. It forgets orientation and sign, but it keeps exactly the information that survives the chapter's homotopy argument. The hypotheses are not cosmetic: compactness, boundary control, and transversality are what make the finite count legal.

title: Boundary Control Blocks Retractions
notes: Use the disk-to-circle schematic to show why parity can obstruct a retraction. A map that is fixed on the boundary would force an intersection count at the boundary that cannot be reconciled with a homotopy through the disk. The point is not the particular drawing but the invariant: the boundary condition prevents the count from escaping.

title: Winding Number Counts Rotating Rays
notes: Winding number is the integer version of the same counting habit. Around a test point off the curve, track the changing argument of the vector from the point to the moving curve. The total angle change is constant on components of the complement and jumps only when a path crosses the curve.

title: Jordan-Brouwer As A Separation Test
notes: Frame Jordan-Brouwer as the higher-dimensional separation statement suggested by winding. An embedded codimension-one sphere has two complementary regions, and crossing the hypersurface changes the component label. The slide keeps the theorem visual while avoiding a full proof.

title: Borsuk-Ulam On The Circle
notes: For the circle case, define the antipodal residual g(theta) equals f(theta) minus f(theta plus pi). The residual reverses sign under a half-turn, so continuity forces a zero. A zero is exactly an antipodal pair with the same scalar value.

title: Antipodal Coincidence In Higher Dimension
notes: Now state the general idea without overloading the proof. If a continuous map from the n-sphere to n-space separated every antipodal pair, the odd difference map would avoid the origin. After normalization it would produce an antipodal self-map with the wrong parity behavior. That is the topological pressure behind Borsuk-Ulam.

title: Where The Counting Argument Breaks
notes: Pause on the failure modes because they are common student mistakes. A nontransverse intersection may not be finite or stable. A noncompact sweep can lose points at infinity. Boundary leakage can change the endpoint count. The mod two invariant is robust only inside the correct geometric fence.

title: Recap: Count What Homotopy Cannot Change
notes: Close by tracing the workflow once more. Build boundary coordinates, classify compact one-manifolds, perturb to transverse position, count the finite set modulo two, and interpret the surviving count as winding, separation, or antipodal coincidence. This workflow prepares the oriented intersection theory in the next chapter.
